# One Concept Across the Stack

The Microsoft agent stack has many surfaces, and each has its own word for "a thing the model can call": action, tool, plugin, connector, function, skill.
ms-rapp/1 reduces them to one concept: **a Step is a function with a schema**. Every surface below already accepts that shape, so one Step file reaches all of them.

## The answer in brief

- A Step's `metadata` is a function schema: a name, a description, a parameters object.
- That one schema can be written out three ways: a **function tool**, an **OpenAPI operation**, or an **MCP tool**.
- Every Microsoft agent surface accepts at least one of the three. None needs the Step to change.

## The three projections

| Projection | Made from | Who accepts it |
|---|---|---|
| Function tool | `metadata` as is (`BasicAgent.to_tool()`) | Brainstem, Foundry function calling, Agent Framework function tools, Agents SDK code |
| OpenAPI operation | `docs/ms-rapp1/openapi.json`, one operation per Step | Copilot Studio REST API tools, Power Platform custom connectors, Foundry OpenAPI tools, Microsoft 365 Copilot API plugins |
| MCP tool | `name`, `description`, and `parameters` as the input schema | Copilot Studio MCP, Microsoft 365 Copilot MCP plugins, Foundry MCP, Agent Framework MCP |

The function tool and the OpenAPI file are built and tested in this repository. The MCP projection is the same three fields under MCP's names; it is described here and not yet built.

## Surface by surface

| Surface | Its word | How a Step arrives |
|---|---|---|
| Brainstem | agent | the file itself, in `agents/` |
| RAPP Runtime | Step | the file itself, in the Step Catalog |
| Copilot Studio | tool (REST API or MCP) | the OpenAPI file; Copilot Studio converts version 3 files to version 2 |
| Power Platform | custom connector | the OpenAPI file |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot | plugin (API or MCP) | the OpenAPI file, or MCP |
| Microsoft Foundry | tool (OpenAPI, function, MCP) | see [[Microsoft Foundry]] |
| Microsoft Agent Framework | function tool, MCP tool | `metadata` as a function, or MCP |
| Microsoft 365 Agents SDK | your agent's code | the agent calls the Step API, or runs `perform` in process |

## Why one concept is enough

Each surface adds hosting, channels, sign-in and governance around the same core: the model reads a schema and calls a function.
Keep the function in one file with one schema and the surfaces become delivery choices, not rewrites.
Change the Step once and every projection is rebuilt from it; `tools/build_ms_rapp1.py --check` fails if the OpenAPI file falls behind.

## Not yet verified

These mappings follow the published shape of each surface, read from Microsoft Learn on 2026-11-01. The generated OpenAPI file has not yet been imported into Copilot Studio, Power Platform, Microsoft 365 Copilot or Foundry, and the MCP projection is not built. Several of these features are in preview.

See also [[Steps]], [[RAPP Runtime]] and [[ms-rapp-1 Overview]].

# RAPP Runtime

**RAPP Runtime** is the ms-rapp/1 engine that runs AI steps.
It has the Brainstem's shape, named in terms enterprise engineers and reviewers already use.

## The answer in brief

- One fixed engine runs every Step. It does not change per use case.
- One signed-in endpoint, the **Step API**, serves every Step. A new capability never adds an endpoint.
- The **Step Catalog** is a folder of reviewed Step files, loaded when they are called.
- Every run leaves a **Run Receipt** for audit.

## Name map

| RAPP Runtime | Brainstem | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| RAPP Runtime | Brainstem kernel | The fixed engine. See [[The Brainstem Kernel]]. |
| Step API | `POST /chat` | `POST /api/lens/<route>`: one endpoint for every Step. |
| Step | `agent.py` | One file, one business task, one checked result. See [[Steps]]. |
| Step Catalog | `agents/` | The approved set of Steps: only reviewed, deployed files. |
| Live catalog | agents reload every request | A merged and deployed Step is used on the next call. |
| Step Policy | `soul.md` | Fixed instructions. The model passes values; the Step checks them. |
| Result | `response` | The checked output, returned as `frame`. |
| Run Receipt | agent logs | Which Step, which model, how many attempts, what usage. |
| Change Control | a pull request into `agents/` | A Step arrives only by reviewed pull request and deploy, never from a browser. |

The code names (`lens`, `/api/lens/<route>`) stay as they are. The enterprise names are documentation names, so no published caller breaks.

## Where the shape differs, on purpose

| | Brainstem `/chat` | Step API |
|---|---|---|
| Input | `{user_input, conversation_history, session_id}` | the Step's own `metadata.parameters` |
| Output | `{response, session_id, ...}` | `{frame}`, matching the Step's `RESULT_SCHEMA` |
| Who picks the agent | the model | the caller, by route |

A Step is a fixed task with structured input. That keeps each Step reviewable on its own, which is what an enterprise release review assesses.
A free-text `/chat` on RAPP Runtime is allowed by the profile, but it accepts open text, so it should go through its own review before release.

See also [[ms-rapp-1 Overview]] and [[Run Receipts and Change Control]].

# Run Receipts and Change Control

Two rules make RAPP Runtime fit an enterprise review: every run leaves a record, and the set of Steps changes only through review.

## The answer in brief

- A **Run Receipt** records each run: the Step, the model, the number of attempts and the usage.
- The **Step Catalog** holds only files that were reviewed and deployed. The runtime never writes or downloads a Step.
- A new Step is a pull request, not a new endpoint and not a new release of the engine.

## Run Receipts

A receipt answers the questions an auditor asks about one AI step:

| Question | Receipt field |
|---|---|
| Which capability ran? | the Step's route and the hash of its file |
| Which model answered? | the model name |
| Did the model's answer pass the Step's checks? | the number of attempts, and the last refusal if any |
| What did it cost? | the token usage |

Receipts record what ran, not the customer's content. Keep payloads out of logs unless the review approves them.

## Change Control

1. A Step is written as a file and opened as a pull request.
2. Review reads one file: its parameters, its result schema, its checks.
3. Merge and deploy put it in the Step Catalog. The next call uses it.

The engine never loads code from a browser, an upload or a model response. This is the same rule app stores apply to apps after review: new behavior arrives as reviewed code.

## When a Step goes back to review

A Step stays inside an existing review when it uses only what the service already uses: the same sign-in, the same model, no new outside system.
A Step that sends email, writes to a new data store or calls a new service is a new data flow and needs its own review.

See also [[RAPP Runtime]], [[Security Considerations]] and [[Conformance and Drift]].

title: Steps
section: ms-rapp-1

# Steps

A **Step** is a rapp/1 agent with two extra fields.
Drop it into a Brainstem's `agents/` folder and it loads like any other agent. RAPP Runtime serves the same file through the Step API.

## The answer in brief

- A Step extends `BasicAgent`, sets `name` and `metadata`, and implements `perform(**kwargs)`, exactly as in [[The Agent Contract]].
- It adds `ROUTE` (its Step API path) and `RESULT_SCHEMA` (the shape of its result).
- A rapp/1 host ignores the two extra fields. That is the whole compatibility story.

## The contract

| Field | rapp/1 | ms-rapp/1 adds | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| file name | `*_agent.py` | | so a Brainstem discovers it |
| class | one `BasicAgent` subclass | | |
| `metadata` | name, description, parameters | | `parameters` is an object schema; it is the Step API request body |
| `perform(**kwargs)` | returns a string | | for a Step, a JSON string matching `RESULT_SCHEMA` |
| `ROUTE` | | yes | 1 to 40 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens |
| `RESULT_SCHEMA` | | yes | a JSON schema object |

`tools/build_ms_rapp1.py --check` enforces these rules on every Step in `docs/ms-rapp1/steps/`.

## The example

`docs/ms-rapp1/steps/action_items_agent.py` lists the action items in meeting notes. It is deterministic, so the tests run it without a model.

```python
ROUTE = "action-items"
RESULT_SCHEMA = {"type": "object", "properties": {"items": {...}}, "required": ["items"]}

class ActionItemsAgent(BasicAgent):
    def __init__(self):
        self.name = "ActionItems"
        self.metadata = {"name": self.name, "description": "...",
                         "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"notes": {"type": "string"}},
                                        "required": ["notes"]}}
        super().__init__(name=self.name, metadata=self.metadata)

    def perform(self, **kwargs):
        ...
        return json.dumps({"items": items})
```

Given the notes `Action: Dana: send the pricing sheet` and `TODO: book the follow-up`, it returns one item owned by Dana and one marked Unassigned.

## Writing a good Step

- **One fixed task.** A Step that does two things is two Steps.
- **Structured in, structured out.** The parameters and the result schema are the review surface.
- **No new systems.** A Step that reaches a new outside service or data store is a new data flow and goes back to review. See [[Run Receipts and Change Control]].

See also [[RAPP Runtime]] and [[Microsoft Foundry]].

# Failure Atlas

A consumer checks every incoming frame in a fixed order.
The **Failure Atlas** maps each check to the failure it usually catches.
Use it to find *where* a frame was refused, then fix the producer.

## The one rule to remember

**The step is a refusal location, not a repair instruction.**

- Correct the producer, or perform an authorized migration.
- Do not change the received frame until it passes.
- When evidence is missing or unverifiable, the consumer **fails closed**. It never turns "could not check" into a pass.

## Frame verification steps

| Step | Consumer checks | Typical failure |
|---|---|---|
| `1` | exact keys, types, grammar, registry values, fixed UTC | dialect, missing/null confusion, malformed field |
| `1a` | `stream_id` equals the stream of record | cross-stream replay |
| `2` | recomputed particle equals `payload_hash` | payload changed |
| `3` | recomputed wave equals `frame_hash` | envelope changed |
| `4` | genesis or contiguous particle chain and nondecreasing UTC | gap, fork, wrong parent, time reversal |
| `5` | swarm `prev_wave` rule; null elsewhere | wrong wire discipline |
| `6` | required/present signature, key binding, tenure, tombstone | missing authorship or unauthorized signer |

## Reading each step in plain words

- **Step 1 — shape.** The frame must have exactly the right fields, types and formats. Extra fields, a different encoding, or a null where a value belongs all fail here. See [[The Frame]] and [[Canonicalization]].
- **Step 1a — right stream.** A valid frame copied into a different stream is refused.
- **Step 2 — payload.** The consumer re-hashes the payload. A mismatch with `payload_hash` means the payload changed. See [[Content Addressing]].
- **Step 3 — envelope.** The consumer re-hashes the unsigned envelope. A mismatch with `frame_hash` means something in the envelope changed. See [[The Wire]].
- **Step 4 — chain.** The frame must be a genesis, or link to the previous frame's particle, with time that does not go backward. Gaps, forks and wrong parents fail here.
- **Step 5 — wire discipline.** Swarm (`net:*`) streams must link `prev_wave`. Other streams must leave it null.
- **Step 6 — signature and authority.** A required signature must be present, bound to a registered key, within its tenure, and not revoked by a tombstone. See [[Trust and Signatures]] and [[The Registry]].

## A common failure outside the frame: the wrong space

Every rapp/1 hash belongs to a named **address space**.
A bare 64-hex digest has no meaning on its own.
Hashing the right bytes in the wrong space gives a different, non-matching address.

| Space | Function |
|---|---|
| `rapp/1:particle` | frame payload address |
| `rapp/1:wave` | unsigned frame-envelope address |
| `rapp/1:rappid` | identity tail |
| `rapp/1:egg` | packed file address inside an egg |
| `rapp/1:egg-manifest` | whole egg identity |
| `rapp/1:seal` | retired-head seal |

When a digest does not match, first ask: **in which space?**

## Related

- [[The Frame]]
- [[Conformance Classes]]
- [[Conformance and Drift]]
- [[Security Considerations]]
- [[Glossary]]

# Glossary

This is the **vocabulary of rapp/1** in one place.
Each term gets a short, plain definition.
The specification text stays authoritative; see [[Sources and Provenance]].

## Identity terms

- **rappid** — the permanent name of a running brainstem, object or door. Format: `rappid:@<owner>/<slug>:<64-lowercase-hex>`. The tail is minted once from UUIDv4 octets or a public key (SPKI DER), never from the owner/slug name. See [[Identity and the Rappid]].
- **identity** — continuity across changing content. In rapp/1, identity is the minted tail of a rappid, not the readable owner/slug.
- **provisional identity** — an older rappid whose tail is not 64 lowercase hex characters. It can be read but must not be emitted. Upgrading it requires owner-authorized re-anchoring.
- **re-anchor** — an owner-authorized identity change for exactly one allowed case: provisional upgrade, key rotation, key compromise, or pre-standard key-tag migration.
- **tombstone** — an owner-signed registry record that revokes a keyed rappid from `revoked_utc` forward.

## Data and hashing terms

- **canonical form** — the one RFC 8785 JCS byte representation of an admissible I-JSON value. See [[Canonicalization]].
- **I-JSON** — the interoperable JSON profile from RFC 7493 that canonicalization is built on.
- **JCS** — JSON Canonicalization Scheme, RFC 8785. It fixes member order, escaping, number form and whitespace.
- **legacy form** — any historical encoding that is not the current canonical form. Live legacy is drift and must be migrated. Sealed re-genesis history is kept as evidence, not as a second dialect.
- **content address** — a SHA-256 digest computed in a named rapp/1 domain. It changes if the content changes. See [[Content Addressing]].
- **domain separation** — prefixing hash input with an exact space tag and a newline, so the same bytes in different roles get different addresses.
- **address space** — a named domain in which a hash has meaning. rapp/1 stores and looks up by `(space, hash)`, never by a bare 64-hex string.

## Event terms

- **frame** — the closed eleven-field event envelope. It carries a payload particle, a whole-frame wave, chain links and an optional signature. See [[The Frame]].
- **particle** — `H("rapp/1:particle", payload)`, stored as `payload_hash`. It addresses what happened.
- **wave** — `H("rapp/1:wave", frame - {frame_hash, sig})`, stored as `frame_hash`. It addresses the exact unsigned envelope. See [[The Wire]].
- **stream** — an append-only sequence of frames sharing one `stream_id`.
- **biography stream** — a stream identified directly by a rappid. It chains particles through `prev`; `prev_wave` is null.
- **swarm stream** — a shared `net:*` stream. It chains particles through `prev` and waves through `prev_wave`, and every frame must be signed.
- **worldline** — the particle-linked history of a brainstem or stream.
- **genesis** — the sequence-zero frame the live chain descends from.
- **head** — the highest verified frame descending from the registered genesis. Consumers keep heads to detect rollback.
- **re-genesis** — the owner-authorized operation that seals an old chain, publishes a new sequence-zero frame, updates the registry and retires the old bytes under `legacy/`.
- **kind** — a registered `noun.verb` event name.

## Packaging and trust terms

- **egg** — a `rapp/1-egg` manifest plus, for tree variants, deterministic stored-ZIP contents. It packages a brainstem, rapplication, session, invite, neighborhood, estate, or sealed ciphertext artifact. See [[The Egg]].
- **registry** — the signed, append-only estate root of trust for keys, kinds, genesis records, re-anchors, tombstones, owner succession and canonical-source pointers. See [[The Registry]].
- **estate** — a governed collection of brainstems and neighborhoods sharing one registry and owner succession.
- **authorship** — the claim that a key signed an artifact. It needs a valid signature, and does not by itself prove the key was authorized. See [[Trust and Signatures]].
- **authority** — the right of a signer to decide at a given time. It comes from the registry and its owner-succession records.
- **integrity** — evidence that bytes or chain links have not changed. Integrity does not imply authorship.
- **freshness** — confidence that signed mutable state is recent enough. A valid registry signature proves authenticity, not freshness.
- **fail closed** — refuse, or report unknown, when evidence is missing, malformed, stale or unverifiable. Never turn "could not check" into a pass.

## Roles

- **producer** — emits only current canonical values, addresses, identities, frames and egg variants.
- **consumer** — validates frames, eggs, signatures, registry state and all refusal conditions before accepting input.
- **router/mirror** — transports or serves artifacts without inventing endpoints or rewriting addressed bytes.

See [[Conformance Classes]] for how these roles are tested.

## Runtime and release terms

- **Grail kernel** — an estate-declared, byte-pinned runtime. Its `grail_id` is `"grail:" || Hb("rapp/1:grail", kernel_bytes)`. Once activated, those bytes are permanent; capabilities grow outside them. See [[The Brainstem Kernel]].
- **release capsule** — the canonical `rapp-cicd/1-release` payload naming one immutable candidate. See [[RAPP CICD]].
- **serving lineage** — the sequence of release identities that have received user traffic.
- **deployment cell** — an independently observable and isolatable runtime failure domain, governed by `rapp-deploy/1`. See [[RAPP Deploy]].

## Address spaces

| Space | Function | Input |
|---|---|---|
| `rapp/1:particle` | frame payload address | canonical value via `H` |
| `rapp/1:wave` | unsigned frame-envelope address | canonical value via `H` |
| `rapp/1:rappid` | identity tail | UUID or SPKI octets via `Hb` |
| `rapp/1:egg` | packed file address inside an egg | raw octets via `Hb` |
| `rapp/1:egg-manifest` | whole egg identity | manifest without `sig` via `H` |
| `rapp/1:seal` | retired-head seal | exact retained head octets via `Hb` |

A bare digest should always prompt one question: **in which space?**

## Notation

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `canonical(v)` | UTF-8 JCS serialization of admissible value `v` |
| `H(space, v)` | SHA-256 of `utf8(space) + 0x0A + canonical(v)` |
| `Hb(space, b)` | SHA-256 of `utf8(space) + 0x0A + raw octets b` |
| `x - {a,b}` | object `x` with exactly members `a` and `b` removed |
| `64hex` | exactly 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters |
| `uint53` | integer from 0 through 2^53−1 |
| SPKI DER | canonical DER encoding of a SubjectPublicKeyInfo public key |

# Sources and Provenance

The protocol notes in this vault are an **authored, plain-language expansion** of the upstream RAPP/1 specification.
They explain the specification. They do not replace it.
When a note and the specification differ, **the specification wins**.

## What the vault draws on

- **Protocol, Operations and Building notes** — expand the upstream RAPP/1 specification and its companion book.
- **Production Guide step notes** — expand the RAPP production guide in this repository, [the production guide](../rapp-guide.html).

Notes drawn only from the production guide carry no upstream pin.

## The pin

Every specification-derived note is pinned to one upstream commit:

`0b24e7d60786d39d97265338add9ca784bf5a7ab`

- The pin means the note was written against that exact version of the specification.
- Newer upstream versions do not change these notes until someone re-reviews them and moves the pin.

## How each note records its source

Every note starts with YAML frontmatter. Two fields carry provenance:

- `source` — the upstream file and section the note expands, for example `SPEC.md §7; book/05-the-frame.md`.
- `upstream_commit` — the pinned commit, for notes drawn from the specification.

Example:

```yaml
source: "SPEC.md §7; book/05-the-frame.md"
upstream_commit: 0b24e7d60786d39d97265338add9ca784bf5a7ab
```

## The build check

A build check reads every note's frontmatter.
**It fails if a specification-derived note loses its pin.**
This keeps every protocol claim traceable to a fixed source.

## The specification text is authoritative

- The vault paraphrases. It may simplify wording for readability.
- Normative rules (MUST, MUST NOT, exact formats) live in the specification.
- Exact identifiers — field names, wire tags such as `rapp/1`, hash space names, file names — are copied verbatim.

If you are implementing, read the specification section named in each note's `source` field.
Start with [[Implementing the Protocol]].
